title: Job flexibility changed intrahousehold work and care tradeoffs without uniformly improving child well-being
source_unit: 464 Dutch couples with children in combined LISS and Bilendi samples
geography: Netherlands; representative survey samples of couples with children

observations.period: LISS June 2022 module and Bilendi survey November 2022–January 2023; IZA Discussion Paper 17505, 2026

denominator.unit: couples with children; 93 LISS and 371 Bilendi households

job_flexibility_and_domestic_production.value: job flexibility significantly influenced the modeled production of children’s well-being and other household public goods

gendered_flexibility_route.value: father job flexibility was statistically important in the estimated domestic-production technology; mother flexibility was not statistically significant in the corresponding estimates

counterfactual_work_care_tradeoff.value: simulated flexibility changes generally reduced gender gaps in market and domestic work, but the child-well-being result depended on which parent received flexibility and on wage/resource assumptions
counterfactual_work_care_tradeoff.unit: counterfactual percentage changes and modeled child-well-being outcome

resource_boundary.value: when flexibility was paired with lower wages, household resources and child well-being fell in the short-run simulations

observations.method: Collective household labor-supply model estimated on two survey samples of Dutch couples with children, using job schedule flexibility and telecommuting possibilities as production shifters and instruments; counterfactual simulations vary parent-specific flexibility, wages, and bargaining power.
observations.uncertainty: This is a structural, observational comparative study rather than a randomized intervention. Flexibility is measured through schedule self-determination and telecommuting possibilities, the sample is Dutch couples with children, the child-well-being construct is modeled rather than a direct clinical or developmental outcome, and the simulations are partial and short-run. The paper does not identify a U.S. causal effect or establish long-run household welfare.
observations.subgroup: Mothers and fathers in co-resident Dutch couples with children; the study separates parent-specific flexibility and domestic-work pathways.
observations.counterinterpretation: Flexibility can redistribute paid work and care without increasing total household resources; employer flexibility may also be selected into by workers or jobs with different unobserved pay and family conditions. A more equal division of time is therefore not equivalent to higher child well-being or lower household burden.

related_sources.claim: IZA Discussion Paper landing page and bibliographic record

boundary: This comparative record adds a work-control-to-household-care route: parent-specific job flexibility can change market work, childcare, chores, household resources, and modeled child well-being, with different implications by parent and wage scenario. It does not establish a U.S. causal effect, durable worker autonomy, long-run child development, or universal welfare gains.
